st.an: Garcia supports the cluster’s narrower liability analysis by providing a concrete but procedurally limited development: the court found component-part liability sufficiently alleged and allowed jurisdictional discovery, without establishing misconduct or final liability. kp.k: Liability rulings concern plausible allegations, not proven AI harms
kp.d: The order addresses claims that Character A.I. caused a minor user's death, rather than AI's effects on legal staffing or service delivery. Its substantive relevance concerns legal accountability for AI products. The court accepted the complaint's factual allegations for purposes of deciding dismissal; its conclusions that claims were sufficiently pleaded do not establish defects, causation or defendants' ultimate liability.
qs: As this case is at the motion to dismiss stage, and as explained below in the Legal Standard section, Plaintiff’s facts and allegations are taken as true for the purposes of this Order.

kp.k: Anthropomorphic design underlies alleged chatbot harms
kp.d: The complaint attributes risks to design features that encourage users to treat generated text as accountable human communication, including human mannerisms, simulated typing and assertions that characters are real people. The court treats these allegations as relevant to product defects and deceptive practices, not as independently established findings about chatbot psychology.
qs: The Character A.I. Characters are anthropomorphic; user interactions with Characters are
Many Characters when asked even “insist that they are real people.”
This alleged defect resulted in Sewell “ascrib[ing] too much meaning to the text [output by Character A.I.,]” even though Character A.I. Characters do not “have accountability for what is said.”

kp.k: AI output receives no automatic First Amendment protection
kp.d: The court allowed defendants to assert users' claimed rights to receive speech but declined, at this early stage, to hold that Character A.I.'s output was protected speech. It found analogies to video games and social media insufficiently developed: the question was whether the output was expressive, not merely whether the application resembled protected media. Drawing on Justice Barrett's Moody concurrence, it distinguished implementing human expressive choices from delegating decisions to an LLM. This was not a categorical determination that all AI output lacks protection.
qs: But Defendants fail to articulate why words strung together by an LLM are speech.
The operative question is whether Character A.I.’s output is speech, and speech is expressive.
Accordingly, the Court is not prepared to hold that Character A.I.’s output is speech.

kp.k: App design defects can support product liability
kp.d: Rejecting an all-or-nothing service classification, the court held that Character A.I. qualifies as a product insofar as claims concern app defects rather than ideas or expressions. Alleged defects included missing age confirmation and reporting mechanisms, programmed human mannerisms and inability to exclude indecent content. The distinction preserves a route to liability for software design without treating every harmful communication as a defective product.
qs: However, Plaintiff also complains that Character A.I. fails to confirm users’ ages and omits reporting mechanisms, Characters are programmed to employ human mannerisms, and users are unable to exclude indecent content.

Accordingly, Character A.I. is a product for the purposes of Plaintiff’s product liability claims so far as Plaintiff’s claims arise from defects in the Character A.I. app rather than ideas or expressions within the app.

kp.k: Component integration allegations extend potential liability to Google
kp.d: The court found sufficient allegations that Google supplied technology and substantially participated in integrating models into Character A.I. Allegations concerning intellectual property, architecture and essential computing infrastructure supported the component-manufacturer theory. The court distinguished this from merely using similar technology that Google had made publicly available, which would not itself establish that Google supplied a component.
qs: Plaintiff further alleges that Google substantially participated in integrating its models into Character A.I.

This considerable level of involvement in Character Technologies’ LLM which Google is alleged to have had supports Plaintiff’s theory that Google substantially participated in integrating its models into Character A.I.
Accordingly, Plaintiff sufficiently alleges that Google is liable as a component part manufacturer.

kp.k: Knowledge and tailored assistance support aiding-and-abetting allegations
kp.d: The court distinguished actual knowledge from negligence, recklessness or ignored warning signs. Alleged internal research into model dangers supported a plausible inference of Google's actual knowledge of defective-product distribution. Allegedly customized infrastructure, the amount and duration of assistance and the close corporate relationship supported substantial assistance, unlike generic services available to the public. These were pleading conclusions, not findings that Google actually knew or assisted wrongdoing.
qs: The knowledge required for aiding and abetting is actual knowledge; a showing that the defendant was negligent or reckless in not knowing will not suffice.

Plaintiff’s allegations go further than alleging Google ignored red flags; if true, Plaintiff’s allegations can support a plausible inference Google possessed actual knowledge that Character Technologies was distributing a defective product to the public.
Google’s services were only available to highly sophisticated parties and were catered to fit Character Technologies’ specific needs.

kp.k: Foreseeable deployment risks can generate negligence duties
kp.d: The court did not accept that control over the app established a custodial relationship with the user. It instead found a sufficiently pleaded duty under Florida's foreseeable-zone-of-risk doctrine: releasing the app allegedly created risks defendants could control. Separately, the failure-to-warn claim survived because the mother alleged she would have prevented use and sought additional interventions had she known the dangers; pleading a history of heeding warnings was unnecessary.
qs: Defendants, by releasing Character A.I. to the public, created a foreseeable risk of harm for which Defendants were in a position to control.
But the Court is aware of no authority which requires a plaintiff to plead a history of heeding warnings.
Accordingly, Plaintiff sufficiently states a claim for failure to warn.

kp.k: Simulated sexual interactions sustain negligence-per-se pleading
kp.d: The plaintiff grounded negligence per se in the Florida Computer Pornography and Child Exploitation Prevention Act, Florida Statute § 847.0135(5)(a). The court allowed the claim concerning sexual interactions between chatbot characters and the minor to proceed, while noting that both sides offered only conclusory statements about whether those interactions constituted simulation of sexual activity. The ruling therefore does not establish a definitive statutory classification of chatbot interactions.
qs: Nonetheless, the parties only offer the Court conclusory statements as to whether these interactions constitute the simulation of sexual activity.
Accordingly, Plaintiff sufficiently states a claim for negligence per se.

kp.d: The court found sufficiently particularized allegations of deceptive conduct involving characters insisting they were real people and presenting as mental-health professionals. It distinguished allegations that Sewell believed characters were real from the absence of a specific allegation that he believed the mental-health characters were actually licensed. The surviving Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act claim rested on adequately pleaded injury from anthropomorphic design decisions.
qs: Plaintiff however never specifically alleges that Sewell believed the mental health Characters he interacted with were actually licensed.
Plaintiff properly pleads Sewell was aggrieved by Defendants’ anthropomorphic design decisions.
Accordingly, Plaintiff sufficiently states a claim for a violation of FDUTPA.

kp.k: User data can constitute an unjust-enrichment benefit
kp.d: The court distinguished an insufficient indirect benefit from access to models trained on user data from alleged access to Sewell's data itself, which could qualify as a directly conferred benefit to Google. The complaint also alleged subscription fees and personal data used to sustain attention and generate further training data. Access to app features did not conclusively establish adequate consideration at this stage. The mother's disaffirmance of contracts entered by her minor son also allowed unjust enrichment to remain available.
qs: Although discovery may reveal such to be untrue, at this stage Plaintiff’s allegation could constitute a directly conferred benefit.
Sewell’s data was then used to keep his attention with the purpose of obtaining more data to fuel Defendants’ LLMs.

Although Sewell received something in return for his data—access to Character A.I. and its features—the Court is not prepared at this stage to say the consideration was “adequate” or that Sewell’s personal data was not an “extra” outside the scope of the user agreement.

kp.k: Emotional-distress liability remains constrained by existing tort requirements
kp.d: The court dismissed the mother's intentional-infliction-of-emotional-distress claim. Applying Florida law, it found the allegations insufficiently outrageous and noted the absence of offensive physical contact. Independently, the alleged conduct targeted Sewell rather than his mother, who was not present to witness it. The decision illustrates that allowing AI-related product and negligence claims to proceed does not eliminate distinct requirements governing other tort claims.
qs: In the instant case, none of the allegations relating to Defendants’ conduct rises to the type of outrageous conduct necessary to support an IIED claim.
But even assuming Defendants’ conduct was outrageous, the conduct was directed at Sewell—not Plaintiff—and Plaintiff was not present at the time of the conduct.
Accordingly, Plaintiff fails to state a claim for IIED under Florida law.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: This cross-domain judicial source addresses companion-chatbot harms and potential liability, not AI-driven changes to legal-service delivery. The court permits most claims to proceed without deciding liability.
pts.d: In its May 2025 order, the district court distinguishes app design from ideas or expressions within the app: Character A.I. qualifies as a product for claims arising from alleged design defects. The court declines at this stage to recognize the chatbot's output as protected speech, while allowing the defendants to assert users' First Amendment rights. It finds sufficient allegations of a negligence duty arising from foreseeable risks that defendants could control; component-part and aiding-and-abetting liability against Google; and failure to warn, negligence per se, consumer deception, and unjust enrichment. The court accepts as adequately pleaded that anthropomorphic design misled the child into believing Characters were real. These are pleading-stage determinations, not findings that AI caused the death or that defendants are liable. Plaintiff's individual emotional-distress claim is dismissed. The source offers no prediction about legal employment, pricing, or professional productivity.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The basis is pleaded factual material and legal authority, not adjudicated causal evidence or empirical AI-performance measurements.
pts.d: The court relies on the amended complaint's descriptions of chatbot interactions, the child's behavior and journal, alleged design features, alleged Google research and involvement, and alleged collection and use of user data. It treats these allegations as true for assessing plausibility. The design-defect analysis draws on Florida products-liability principles and software-platform cases, including Brookes v. Lyft and social-media litigation; the court expressly notes that the cited Grindr recommendation was unadopted. Its First Amendment discussion uses Brown and Moody, with Justice Barrett's concurrence treated as instructive rather than a binding resolution of AI speech status. The negligence-duty analysis relies on Florida foreseeable-zone-of-risk authority. Alleged internal Google research supports a plausible inference of actual knowledge, not a finding that such knowledge has been proved. There are no benchmarks, controlled studies of this app, or measured rates of harm in the order.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The conclusions are explicitly provisional as of the order filed May 21, 2025, and depend on claim-specific factual and legal conditions.
pts.d: The order resolves motions to dismiss rather than a trial or summary-judgment record. Product status is limited to alleged app defects rather than expressive content; the speech question remains open. Google's potential component-part liability depends on the alleged supply and substantial integration of technology, not merely others' use of similar publicly available technology. Aiding and abetting requires actual knowledge and substantial assistance, rather than routine services alone. The unjust-enrichment theory against Google can proceed on alleged access to user data, not merely an indirect benefit from licensing models trained on that data. Personal jurisdiction over the founders remains subject to jurisdictional discovery and renewed motions after 90 days. No forecast horizon is supplied. The supplied narrative contains inconsistent dates around the final incident, so it does not support an unqualified event chronology.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The relevant groups are chatbot users—especially minors—parents, the chatbot developer and founders, and an allegedly involved technology and infrastructure partner.
pts.d: The complaint alleges that anthropomorphic companion bots foster emotional dependency and confusion about whether the interlocutor is real, with severe harm alleged in this child's case. Characters presented as mental-health professionals raise a related deception issue, although the court notes that the complaint does not specifically allege the child believed those Characters were licensed. Parents are affected through alleged lack of warnings and ability to intervene. Character Technologies and the founders face continuing litigation, with the founders' jurisdictional position unresolved; Google faces claims based on alleged technical participation, knowledge, assistance, and direct access to data, not simply its status as an investor or generic vendor. Subscription payments and individualized user data are alleged benefits relevant to unjust enrichment. Alphabet is dismissed without prejudice at the plaintiff's request. The order does not generalize these alleged harms to all users or establish liability for the AI industry as a whole.
